en: The *Aśokāvadāna* and the *Pāṃśupradānāvadāna*:
he who, having performed sacrifices with his own flesh and limbs, practiced austerities for a long time out of compassion for the welfare of the world.
In order to bring that exertion to fruition, you virtuous ones, listen with focused attention to what is being spoken now.
"Thus have I heard: at one time the Blessed One was dwelling in Śrāvastī"—thus the sūtra should be recited.

Herein, first of all, for those whose thick layers of mud consisting of passion, hatred, delusion, intoxication, pride, deceit, and guile have been swept away by the falling showers of the flowing waters of speech issuing from the opening of the cloud-like mouth of the Blessed Tathāgata...

In the presence of the Gurus—who have dispelled the darkness of false doctrines through the lamp of wisdom born from contemplating the meaning of the treatises on grammar, logic, and other sciences; who are intent upon drinking the water of the sublime Dharma, which excels all else in severing the thirst for cyclic existence; and whose unimpeded teaching cannot be resisted even by Śakra, Brahmā, Īśāna, Yama, Varuṇa, Kubera, Vāsava, Soma, Āditya, and the rest—a hero who crushes the pride of Kandarpa, [I praise him] as the most excellent of all instructors.
Beginning with the Great Being, the Elder Upagupta, who possessed exceedingly great supernormal powers, we shall recall a certain religious discourse that inspires clarity of mind in the wise.
In this regard, you, my teachers, must listen with attentive ears.
Thus it is heard: when the Blessed One, at the time of his final nirvāṇa, having converted the nāga Apalāla, the potter woman, the Caṇḍālī woman, and Gopālī, arrived at Mathurā.
Thereupon the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda:
"Ānanda, in this city of Mathurā, one hundred years after my final parinirvāṇa, there will be a perfumer named Gupta.
He will have a son named Upagupta, who, though not possessing the [physical] marks of a Buddha, will perform the work of a Buddha for me one hundred years after my final parinirvāṇa."
Through his instruction, many monks will realize arhatship by abandoning all defilements;
they will fill a cave eighteen cubits in length and twelve cubits in width with tally-sticks each measuring only four finger-breadths.
Ānanda, this monk Upagupta shall be the foremost among my disciples as instructors.
"Do you see, Ānanda, that dark-blue line of clouds in the distance?
"I do, Venerable Sir.
"Ānanda, this is the mountain named Urūmuṇḍa."
One hundred years after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, there will be a monk named Śāṇakavāsī.
He will establish a monastery here on Mount Urūmuṇḍa and will ordain Upagupta.
Ānanda, in Mathurā there will be two brothers, merchants named Naṭa and Bhaṭa;
they will establish a monastery on Mount Urumuṇḍa,
and it shall be known as the Naṭabhaṭika.
"It will become known as such.
Ānanda, this Naṭabhaṭikā forest retreat shall be for me the foremost of all resting places conducive to tranquility.
Then the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
"It is wonderful, Venerable Sir, that the venerable Upagupta will perform such great benefit for many people.
The Blessed One said, "Not now alone, Ānanda."
Just as in the past, even with his body fallen right here, he performed great benefit for many beings;
on Mount Urumuṇḍa there are three sides,
and in one region five hundred pratyekabuddhas dwell.
In the second [assembly] there were five hundred sages;
in the third, five hundred monkeys.
Among them, that leader of the five hundred monkeys left his troop and went to the side where the five hundred pratyekabuddhas resided.
Upon seeing those Pratyekabuddhas, faith arose within him. He offered them withered leaves, roots, and fruits;
and whenever they sat down cross-legged, he would take his place at the end of the row of elders and proceed until he reached the end of the novices, where he too sat down cross-legged.
When those Pratyekabuddhas had passed into parinirvāṇa,
he offered them withered leaves, roots, and fruits;
they did not accept them.
He pulled at the corners of their robes and grasped their feet,
until the monkey thought to himself:
"They will certainly have passed away.
Then that monkey, having grieved and lamented, went to the second side where five hundred ṛṣis were dwelling.
And those sages were some who relied on thorns, some who relied on ashes, some with their arms raised, and some who stood exposed to the five fires.
He began to disturb their various modes of conduct (*īryāpatha*):
he pulled out the thorns of those who relied on thorns.
He shakes off the ashes of those who rely on ashes;
he causes the downward hand to fall for those with hands raised upward;
and he scatters fire upon those standing in the five fires.
And when their posture was disturbed, he then sat cross-legged before them;
this was reported by those sages to the teacher, and he too spoke thus:
"Sit in the cross-legged posture. When those five hundred rishis had sat down in the cross-legged posture,
they— without a teacher and without instruction— brought the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment to manifestation and realized individual awakening.
Then it occurred to those Pratyekabuddhas:
"Whatever excellence we have attained, all of that is due to this monkey.
Thus, they nourished that monkey with fruits and roots.
And when he had passed away, his body was cremated with fragrant wood.
What do you think, Ānanda? That leader of the five hundred monkeys was this very Upagupta.
Even then, despite having a body that had fallen into ruin, he performed great benefit for many people right here on Mount Urumuṇḍa.
In the future time as well, when I have passed into parinirvāṇa for a hundred years, he will bring about the welfare of many people right here on Mount Urumuṇḍa;
and we shall demonstrate how that will come to pass.
Regarding the account of Śāṇakavāsin:
when the elder Śāṇakavāsin established a monastery on Mount Urumuṇḍa, he took it into consideration.
"Has this perfumer already been born,
or has he not yet been born?
He perceives that he has been born.
As he reflected,

he considered: "That son of his named Upagupta, who was designated as a Buddha without the [physical] marks, who shall perform the work of a Buddha after I have passed into parinirvāṇa for a hundred years— has he been born?"
"Even now it has not arisen.
He saw that even now it had not arisen;
by whatever means he was protected, the perfumer was inspired with faith in the Blessed One's teaching.
When he had gained faith, the Elder entered his house on one day together with many bhikṣus; on another day, accompanied by only one companion;
and on yet another day, alone.
When Gupta the perfumer saw the Elder Śāṇakavāsin alone, he said,
"Does the Noble One have no attendant monk at all?
The Elder replied:
For us who are subject to old age, how could there be a junior attendant?
If anyone goes forth [into homelessness] preceded by faith, [they may do so].
"They shall become our junior monks.
Guptagāndhika said,
"Noble one, for my part, I am still attached to the household life and delight in the objects of the senses."
"I am not able to go forth;
however, whichever son is born to us, we shall give him to the Noble One as a junior attendant.
The Elder said:
"My child, let it be so;
however, you must remember your firm vow.
Meanwhile, a son was born to the perfumer Gupta.
He was given the name Aśvagupta. When he had grown up, the Elder Śāṇakavāsī went to the perfumer Gupta and said,
"Child, you made a promise that whichever son should be born to you, we would give him to the Noble One as his attendant monk."
"And this son has been born;
give me your permission, for I shall cause him to go forth.
The perfumer said:
"Noble one, this is our only son. Please forgive us; whatever second son we may have, we shall give him to you as a junior attendant."
The Elder Śāṇakavāsī focused his attention:
"Is this Upagupta?
He saw that it was not.
The elder said, "So be it.
When his second son was born,
he was given the name Dhanagupta.
When he too had grown up, the Elder Śāṇakavāsī said to Gupta the perfumer:
"Child, you made a promise that whichever son should be born to you, we would give him to the Noble One as a junior attendant (paścācchramaṇa).
And this son has now been born to you."
"Give me your permission; I shall go forth [into the religious life]. The perfumer said, "Noble sir, please be patient; let one of us manage the external affairs."
"The second shall provide protection within the house;
however, whichever shall be our third son, he is given to you, Noble One."
The Elder Śāṇakavāsī focused his attention:
"Is this Upagupta?
He saw that it was not.
Then the elder said,
"So be it.
In the meantime, the third son of the perfumer Gupta was born.
He was handsome, beautiful to behold, and pleasing; he surpassed human appearance yet had not fully attained divine appearance.
After performing an extensive birth festival for him at his birth, they gave him the name Upagupta.
When he had grown up and reached maturity, the Elder Śāṇakavāsī went to the perfumer Gupta and said:
"My child, you made a vow that whichever of our sons becomes the third shall be given by us to the Noble One as a *paścācchramaṇa*.
This third son of yours has now been born;
give him leave, for I shall cause him to go forth."
Gupta the perfumer said, "Noble sir, on agreement:
when there will be profit without interruption, then I shall grant permission."
When he had made that agreement, Māra caused the entire city of Mathurā to be filled with fragrances;
all those inhabitants of Mathurā then purchased perfumes from Upagupta.
He gave away abundant gifts until the Elder Śāṇakavāsī went into the presence of Upagupta,
who was standing at the perfume shop.
He conducted his business according to the law and sold perfumes. He was addressed by the Elder Śāṇakavāsin:
"My child, what kind of mental states and mental factors are arising in you? Are they afflicted or unafflicted?
Upagupta replied:
"Noble one, I do not know at all what kind of mental states and mental factors are afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) and what kind are unafflicted (*akliṣṭa*.
The Elder Śāṇakavāsī said,
"Child, if you are able to fully comprehend the mind alone, you will be able to release it from its counteractive factors (*pratipakṣa*)."
Therefore, he gave him two strips of cloth, one black and one white, with these instructions:
"If a defiled thought arises, place the black strip;
if an undefiled thought arises, place the white strip."
"Direct your mind toward the foul and cultivate the recollection of the Buddha.
Thus was he instructed by him.
As long as his initiated, non-afflicted mental states and mental factors continue to function,
he sets aside two portions of the black [actions] and one portion of the white [actions].
He sets aside half for the black ones and half for the white ones;
eventually, he sets aside two parts for the white ones.
One [thought] is black;
thus, in due order, all thoughts eventually arise as white.
He then establishes a row of only white strips.
He conducts his business according to the law.
In Mathurā, there was a courtesan named Vāsavadattā;
her maidservant went to the presence of Upagupta and purchased perfumes from him.
She was told by Vāsavadattā:
"Girl, that perfumer is being cheated by you;
you bring back many perfumes."
The girl said:
"Noble daughter, Upagupta, the son of a perfumer, is endowed with beauty and possessed of skill and charm; he conducts his business according to the Dharma."
Upon hearing this, a heart full of passion arose in Vāsavadattā toward Upagupta;
she then sent a maidservant to Upagupta with the message:
"I shall come to you."
"I wish to experience pleasure with you.
When this was reported to Upagupta by the maidservant,
Upagupta said:
"Sister, it is not the right time for you to see me.
Vāsavadattā was being entertained with five hundred purāṇas;
then, a thought occurred to her.
She was certainly unable to give even five hundred purāṇas.
Therefore, she sent a maidservant to Upagupta with the message:
"I have no need for even a single kārṣāpaṇa from my noble son."
"I would experience pleasure only with the noble son.
Thus did the maidservant inform him.
Upagupta said:
"Sister, it is not the right time for you to see me.
Meanwhile, a certain son of a merchant entered Vāsavadattā’s presence,
and another caravan leader arrived at Mathurā from the northern region, bringing five hundred horses for sale.
He asked,
"Which courtesan is the most preeminent?
and he heard that it was Vāsavadattā.
Taking five hundred *purāṇas* and many gifts, he went into the presence of Vāsavadattā.
Then, drawn by greed, Vāsavadattā had that merchant’s son killed, threw him into a refuse heap, and enjoyed pleasure with the caravan leader.
Meanwhile, that merchant’s son—
His kinsmen, having pulled him out from the refuse heap, reported it to the king.
Thereupon the king commanded:
"Go, sirs, cut off Vāsavadattā's hands, feet, ears, and nose, and cast her into the cremation ground."
When they had cut off Vāsavadattā’s hands, feet, ears, and nose, and abandoned her in the cremation ground,
Upagupta heard that Vāsavadattā had been cut of her hands, feet, ears, and nose, and abandoned in the cremation ground;
thereupon, a thought arose in him.
Previously, she desired a sight of me for the sake of sensual pleasure;
but now her hands, feet, ears, and nose have been cut off.
Now, however, is the time for her to see me. And he said:
When her limbs were draped in exquisite garments and adorned with various ornaments,
even the sight of her would not have been for the welfare of those seeking liberation who are averse to worldly rebirth.
But now is the time to behold her natural form, as it is destined by its own nature, once she has been deprived of pride, passion, and joy, and wounded by the sharp sword.
Meanwhile, a single boy-servant, carrying a parasol and maintaining a perfectly tranquil deportment, arrived at the cremation ground.
A female attendant of his, out of affection for her former virtues, remained nearby to ward off crows and other scavengers;
she then informed Vāsavadattā.
"O noble daughter, he for whose sake you have sent me to his presence again and again—here is that Upagupta who has arrived.
Surely he must have come here afflicted by lust.
Upon hearing this, Vāsavadattā said:
Seeing me with my beauty destroyed, afflicted by grief, and stained with blood upon the ground, how could he still feel lustful desire?
Then he said to the female messenger,
"Join together those hands, feet, ears, and nose that were cut from my body.
Having joined them, she covered them with a cloth bandage.
Upagupta arrived and stood before Vāsavadattā.
Then, seeing Upagupta standing before her, Vāsavadattā said:
"Noble son, when my body was healthy and well-suited to the pleasures of the senses, I sent messengers to you, noble son, again and again."
The noble son said,
"Sister, it is not the right time for you to see me.
Now my hands, feet, ears, and nose have been cut off.
She remained standing in a mire of her own blood.
"Why have you come now? she asked. And he said:
"This [body] which was once as tender as the interior of a lotus and adorned with costly garments and ornaments—"
At that time, my body was not fit for you to behold; thus you were not seen by me, unfortunate as I am.
Why have you come here now to see me, when my body is no longer fit for sight—
devoid of play, delight, joy, and wonder, terrifying, and smeared with the mire of blood?
Upagupta said:
"Sister, I have not come into your presence afflicted by desire; rather, I have come to perceive the true nature of impure desires."
Though you were concealed by various external garments, ornaments, and other things that are conducive to passion,
even as you were being watched with great effort, it was as if you had not been seen at all.
But this form of yours is visible; it stands in its own nature, devoid of any [permanent] construction.
Those who take delight in this common, putrid thing are unwise and are to be censured.

Who indeed would take delight in this body, which is bound by skin, drenched in blood, covered with hide, plastered over with thick flesh, and enveloped on all sides by thousands of veins? And why? From what source could such attachment arise?
Moreover, sister: having seen forms that are beautiful on the outside, the fool becomes attached;
but knowing them to be corrupt within, the wise man becomes dispassionate.
For even a corpse, whether discarded or not discarded, is indeed impure;
yet those possessed by desire perceive it as pure, conceiving the gratification of their desires to be auspicious.

For in this world, the foul odor arising from the source of impurities is warded off by various kinds of perfumes; and its deformity is concealed externally by various ornaments such as garments and the like.

Sweat, moisture, impurities, and the like are also impure; it is by means of water that one removes them, yet this foul receptacle of excrement is frequented by those whose souls are possessed by desire.

But those who listen to the well-spoken words of the Perfectly Awakened One and put them into practice abandon desires— which give rise to toil, grief, and suffering, and are always censured by the wise— and,
with minds liberated from the cause of desire, they depart for the peaceful forest.
They cross to the further shore of the great ocean of existence by relying on the boat of the path.
Having heard this, Vāsavadattā, distressed by the cycle of existence and with her heart captivated by the recollection of the Buddha’s qualities, said:
"It is so; everything is exactly as the wise man says."
But having properly approached you, I have heard the word of the Buddha.
When Upagupta had delivered a gradual discourse to Vāsavadattā and revealed the truths,

and when he had understood the nature of Vāsavadattā’s own body, he became free from passion for the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*). Through his own teaching of the Dharma, Vāsavadattā attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*) upon the realization of the truths, while Upagupta himself attained the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*).
Then Vāsavadattā, having seen the truth, spoke to Upagupta while inspiring him with deep devotion:
"By your power, the most terrible path to the lower realms, fraught with many evils, has been closed;
the highly meritorious path to heaven and the way to Nirvāṇa have been opened and attained by me."
Furthermore, he said: "I go for refuge to that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One; and to the Dharma, and to the Saṅgha of monks."
I go for refuge to the Victor, whose eyes are as pure and white as a blossomed fresh lotus,
who is accompanied by gods and wise men, and to the Sangha of those free from passion.

When Upagupta had instructed Vāsavadattā with a discourse on the Dharma and departed, not long after he had left, Vāsavadattā passed away and was reborn among the gods. The deities then announced this news in Mathurā.
Having heard the teaching of the Dharma from Upagupta, Vāsavadattā perceived the Noble Truths;
it was reported that she had passed away and been reborn among the gods.
Upon hearing this, the people residing in Mathurā performed funeral rites for the body of Vāsavadattā.
When the Elder Śāṇakavāsī approached Gupta the perfumer, he said, "Give me permission; I shall ordain Upagupta.
Gupta the perfumer replied:
"Noble one, this is the agreement:
when there will be neither gain nor loss, then I shall grant permission.
Thereupon, the Elder Śāṇakavāsin empowered it through his supernatural power such that there was neither gain nor loss.
Then Gupta the perfumer counted, weighed, and measured;
he saw neither profit nor loss.
Thereupon, the Elder Śaṇakavāsī said to Gupta the perfumer:
"For this one has been designated by the Blessed Buddha:
'After I have passed into parinirvāṇa for a hundred years, he will perform the work of a Buddha. Grant me permission; I shall ordain him."
When he had been granted permission by Gupta the perfumer,
the Elder Śāṇakavāsin then led Upagupta to the Naṭabhaṭika forest hermitage.
He was ordained, and the formal act consisting of a motion followed by three proclamations was finalized.
Then, through the abandonment of all defilements, Upagupta realized arhatship. Thereupon, the Elder Śāṇakavāsin said:
"Child Upagupta, you have been designated by the Blessed One: 'One hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, there will be a monk named Upagupta,
a Buddha without the marks,
who shall perform the work of a Buddha for me one hundred years after my parinirvāṇa.'"
"Ānanda, this Upagupta, the monk, is the foremost among my disciples as instructors.
Now, my child, act for the benefit of the Teaching.
Upagupta replied:
"So be it," he replied; thereupon, he was requested to listen to the Dharma,
and a report spread throughout Mathurā.
"Today the Buddha named Upagupta, who is without the [major] marks, will teach the Dharma.
Having heard this, many hundreds of thousands of living beings went out.
Then, the Elder Upagupta entered meditative absorption and surveyed the situation.
How is the assembly seated before the Tathāgata?
He sees that the assembly is situated in the shape of a half-moon.
As he looks further, he considers how the Dharma teaching was delivered by the Tathāgata.
Having delivered the discourse on what was to be done previously, he revealed the Truths;
he too, having delivered the discourse on what was to be done previously, began to reveal the Truths.
And Māra released a rain of pearl necklaces upon that assembly.
The minds of those to be converted were thrown into confusion;
not even a single person attained the vision of the Truth.
When the Elder Upagupta looked about,
wondering who had caused this distraction,
he saw that it was Māra.
Then, on the second day, a vast multitude of people went forth;
Upagupta taught the Dharma,
and a rain of pearl necklaces fell.

When, on the second day as well, the Elder Upagupta had delivered his customary introductory discourse and begun to reveal the Truths, Māra released a rain of gold upon that assembly; the minds of those to be converted were thus distracted,
so that not even a single person attained the vision of the Truths.
When the Elder Upagupta looked around to see who had caused this distraction,
he saw that it was the Evil Māra.
When the third day arrived, a vast multitude of people went forth;
Upagupta was teaching the Dharma,
and a rain of pearls and a rain of gold were falling.
When the third day arrived, the Elder Upagupta, having delivered his discourse on the duties to be performed beforehand, began to proclaim the Truths; meanwhile,
Māra commenced a theatrical performance not far away,
and celestial musical instruments were sounded.
Divine apsarases began to dance;
meanwhile, the assembly of people, though free from passion, was drawn away by Māra upon seeing divine forms and hearing divine sounds.
Thus, Māra drew away Upagupta’s assembly.
With a joyful mind, Māra bound a garland upon the head of the Elder Upagupta;
then the Elder Upagupta began to reflect.
"Who is this? Māra saw him, and a thought arose in his mind.
"This Māra is causing great distraction within the Blessed One's teaching.
For what reason has he not been disciplined by the Blessed One?
[The Blessed One] perceives: 'He is one who is to be disciplined by me.'"
And because of his discipline and his assistance to sentient beings, the Blessed One has declared me to be a Buddha without marks. Then the Elder Upagupta reflected:
"Has the time for his conversion arrived, or not?"
Seeing that the time for those to be converted had arrived,
the Elder Upagupta then took three corpses:
the corpse of a snake, the corpse of a dog, and the corpse of a human.
Having manifested a flower garland through his supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), he approached Māra;
and upon seeing him, joy arose in Māra,
thinking, "Upagupta has been drawn by me."
Then Māra presented his own body; the Elder Upagupta bound it himself. Thereupon, the Elder Upagupta fastened a snake carcass upon Māra’s head.
There was a dog’s carcass around his neck and a human corpse clinging to his ears;
then, having touched them, he said:
"Just as this garland, so repugnant to monks, has been fastened upon me by you."
"This corpse, which is repulsive to those who desire, has been bound by me for you."
Display whatever strength you possess, for today you have encountered the Son of the Buddha.
Even the ocean water, though its surface is agitated with waves tossed by the wind, turns back within the hollows of Mount Malaya.
Then Māra began to remove that corpse;
yet even though he himself entered [the body], he was unable to remove it, like an ant attempting to move the king of mountains.
Becoming indignant, he leapt into the air and said:
If I myself am unable to release my own corpse from my throat,
then other gods of even greater splendor than I shall indeed release it.
The Elder said:
"Seek refuge with Brahmā, or with Indra, the performer of a hundred sacrifices; or enter the blazing fire, or the ocean.
Yet this corpse situated in the throat shall suffer neither moisture, nor desiccation, nor dissolution here."
Having approached the gods—Mahendra, Rudra, Upendra, Draviṇeśvara, Yama, Varuṇa, Kuvera, Vasu, and the rest—he went to Brahmā still without having accomplished his purpose. And he was told by him:
"Forgive me, dear child!

By a disciple of the One Possessing the Ten Powers, the boundary of the end of things has been established by his own supernatural power; who is able to break it, any more than one can breach the shore of the ocean?"
One might perhaps lift up the Himalayas, bound with threads from lotus stalks;
but I shall never remove this dog's carcass clinging to your neck.
Granted that I too possess great strength, nevertheless, I am not equal to the strength of the Son of the Tathāgata.
It is certainly not that there is no fire among those who are radiant; however, the splendor belonging to the solar orb does not exist within the sacrificial fire.
Māra said:
"What do you command now?
To whom shall I go for refuge?"
Brahmā said:
"Go quickly for refuge to that very one, by encountering whom you have fallen from prosperity, power, fame, and happiness;
for whatever being here on the surface of the earth has fallen, he rises up again by relying upon the earth."
Then Māra, perceiving the power of the Tathāgata’s disciples, reflected:
"If even the disciples' teaching is honored by Brahmā,
who indeed could possibly measure the power of that Buddha?"
If he had desired to act otherwise, what instruction would that one of excellent vows not have been capable of giving? But because he did not do so through patience, I have been protected by him.
What need is there for much?
Today I recognize the great compassion of that Sage, whose nature is supreme loving-kindness and whose mind is liberated from all calamities, possessing the luster of a mountain of gold.
For though I was tormented here and there by various arguments by that one blinded by delusion,
even so, I was not made to hear anything unpleasant by him, despite his power.

Then Māra, the lord of the desire realm, realizing that there was no other course for him except through Upagupta, cast everything aside, approached the Elder Upagupta, prostrated at his feet, and said:
"Venerable sir, is it unknown to you how hundreds of offenses against the Blessed One were committed by me, beginning from the foot of the Bodhi tree? Why [is this so]?
When he encountered me in the village of Śālā, that Gautama—"
Even when deprived of food, he did nothing unpleasant to me.
Having become a cow, then staying like a snake, and having assumed the form of a cartman,
that Lord was exhausted by me, yet I was not harmed by him.
But by you, O Hero, having indeed abandoned innate compassion,
I have today been mocked among the worlds of gods and asuras.
The Elder said:
"O wicked one, how is it that you, without even investigating, equate a disciple with the majesty of the Tathāgata?
Do you here seek to bring Mount Meru into parity with a mustard seed?"
Like a firefly compared to the sun in one's cupped hands, the ocean is [vastly superior];
for the compassion of the One Possessing the Ten Powers toward living beings is indeed different—
O gentle one, a disciple does not possess such great compassion.
Moreover,
we have directly perceived this very reason for which the Blessed One forgave even one who had committed an offense.
Māra said:

"Speak, speak! Tell me the disposition of that illustrious one who, guarding his vows through patience, seeks to sever attachment—that man whom I have constantly tormented out of delusion, yet who has looked upon me with a mind of loving-kindness."
The Elder said:
"Listen, gentle one, for you have repeatedly stumbled before the Blessed One."

And there is no other way to wash away the unwholesome states planted against the Buddhas than through faith in the Tathāgata alone. Seeing this very reason, that far-sighted one did not speak anything unpleasant to you here, but rather caused you to obtain only what is pleasing.
By this reasoning, devotion has been generated in your heart by that one of supreme intelligence;
for even a slight amount of devotion toward this [teaching] yields the fruit of liberation for those possessed of wisdom.
Whatever sin you have committed here, O Sage, through a mind blinded by delusion, [has been purified].
All that has been washed away by the flowing streams of the water of faith residing within your heart.
Then Māra, with the hair on his body standing on end like a kadamba flower, prostrated himself with his whole body and said:

But cast off this ornament of the great seer’s wrath, which hangs around your neck out of misplaced friendliness.

Māra, filled with agitation, said:

You yourself understand that I went forth into homelessness after the Blessed One had entered final nirvana a hundred years ago;
by me, the Dharma-body of that Lord of the Three Worlds was seen,

Fie upon that pitiless impermanence which shatters even such forms as these!

With mindfulness focused upon the Buddha, his mind became so intensely attached that he clearly perceived himself as seeing the Blessed One;

For with his face he surpasses the lotus, with his eye the blue water-lily,

That which has been purified by the Arhat through the restraint of giving, patience, meditative concentration, and wisdom— arising from speech, body, and mind— over hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons;

seeing which even an enemy would be filled with joy, how much more so one such as I?

that Upagupta by name had been designated by the Blessed One as the foremost of instructors,

And he reached the world of gods, asuras, and humans, which delights in the most excellent discourses on the Dharma and is indeed liberated in nature.
When the Blessed One had set out upon the royal highway,

While they were playing with sandcastles—

When the boy Jaya, thinking "I shall give some flour," threw a handful of dust into the Blessed One’s bowl,
Vijaya, with palms joined in reverence, expressed his approval; and he will say:
Having seen the Greatly Compassionate One, the Self-Existent, whose entire body was illuminated by a fathom-wide radiance,

Having presented it to the Blessed One, he began to make a formal aspiration:

Then the Sage, having observed his disposition and having fully understood the boy’s sincere vow,
and seeing that the desired fruit would be realized through the power of the field, took up the dust out of compassion.
Because he had projected such wholesome karma as would result in sovereignty,
the Blessed One displayed a smile.
It is indeed the nature of things that whenever the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, manifest a smile,
at that moment rays of light— blue, yellow, red, white, madder-colored, crystal, and silver— issue forth from their mouths;
some go upward, while others go downward.
Those who go downward, having gone to Sañjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Tapana, Pratāpana, and as far as the Avīci hells, fall into those cold hells becoming warm,
and into those hot hells becoming cool.
By that means, the specific causes of suffering for those beings are stilled,
and they think to themselves: "Have we indeed passed away from here, or have we been reborn elsewhere?"
By which our particular afflictions were stilled;
for the sake of generating faith in them, the Blessed One sends forth an emanation,
and they think thus:
"We have not passed away, nor have we been reborn elsewhere;
rather, by the power of this unprecedented being, our particular sufferings have been stilled.
Having developed faith in their minds toward the emanation, they exhaust the karma that leads to hellish rebirth and take up new existence among gods and humans.
Therein they become vessels for the truths.
Those who go upward [pass through] the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Thirty-three, the Yāma, the Tuṣita, the Nirmāṇarati,
the Paranirmitavaśavartin, the Brahmakāyika, the Brahmapurohita, the Mahābrahmā, the Parīttābha, and the Apramāṇābha.

Having gone to the gods ending with the Ābhāsvara, Parīttaśubha, Apramāṇaśubha, Śubhakṛtsna, Anabhraka, Puṇyaprasava, Bṛhatphala, Abṛha, Atapa, Sudṛśa, Sudarśana, and Akaniṣṭha, they proclaim: "Impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self."
And they recite these two verses:
"Exert yourselves! Go forth! Apply yourselves to the teaching of the Buddha!
Shake off the army of Death as an elephant shakes down a reed-thicket!"
For whoever shall practice vigilantly within this Dharma and Vinaya,

Then those rays, having circled the trichiliocosm—the great trichiliocosm world-system—followed after the Blessed One.
If the Blessed One desired to declare a past deed, they vanished behind him; if he desired to declare a future deed, they vanished in front of him;
if he desired to declare rebirth in hell, they vanished into the soles of his feet.
If he wishes to prophesy rebirth among animals, they disappear into his heels; if he wishes to prophesy rebirth among hungry ghosts, they disappear into his big toes;

Then those rays of light, having circumambulated the Blessed One three times, vanished into the palm of the Blessed One’s left hand.
Then the Venerable Ānanda, with palms joined in reverence, spoke this verse:

Free from agitation, having abandoned both dejection and pride, the Buddhas are the supreme causes for the world;
these Conquerors, who have vanquished all enemies, do not display a smile as white as a conch shell or a lotus stalk without a cause.

The world desires prosperity;
so, taking his daughter with him, he went to Pāṭaliputra.

"This is indeed a blessed and praiseworthy celestial maiden," they said;

Thereupon, a thought arose among the women of the harem.

She replied,

She replied,

He played, took pleasure, and enjoyed himself with her.

She replied:
Upon the birth of this boy, I became free from sorrow; therefore, the name Aśoka was given to him. Then a second son was born.
Born when his grief had departed, he was given the name Vītaśoka; Aśoka, however, had limbs that were unpleasant to the touch and was not favored by King Bindusāra.
Then King Bindusāra, desiring to test the prince, addressed the wandering mendicant Piṅgalavatsājīva:

The wandering mendicant Piṅgalavatsājīva said:

When the king, having taken the princes with him, had gone out to the Suvarṇamaṇḍapa park,

"Shall I go there?
She said,

And Rādhagupta, the son of the chief minister, said to him,

Today, the king is testing the princes in the Suvarṇamaṇḍapa garden.

When the food for the princes had been brought,
a vessel of rice mixed with curd was also sent by Aśoka’s mother in an earthenware dish.

And he thought:
"King Aśoka will come to power,
and this man is not favored by the king."
"If I say that Aśoka will become king, I shall have no life remaining.
He spoke thus.
"I shall explain by way of non-distinction from the gods.
The king said:
"Explain this without making distinctions.

The thought occurred to each of them individually:

The king said, "Teacher, examine him further for a while."
The wandering mendicant Piṅgalavatsājīva said,

"My seat shall be the foremost.

Aśoka said:
"It was prophesied without distinction:

"As I see it, I shall become king;
my vehicle shall be the back of an elephant, the earth my seat, and my food shall consist of earthenware vessels, rice porridge with curd sauce, and water for drink.
Thereupon, the wandering mendicant Piṅgalavatsājīva began to court Aśoka’s mother, thinking, "Aśoka will become king."
When she asked,

he replied:
"Aśoka.
She said to him, "Perhaps the king might question you persistently at some point."
"Go, take refuge in a border region;
when you hear that Aśoka has become king, then you must return.
Thus he departed and took up residence in the frontier provinces.
Now, King Bindusāra’s city named Takṣaśilā was in rebellion;
thereupon King Bindusāra dispatched Aśoka,

"Put on your armor! The fourfold army has been granted,

When Prince Aśoka was departing from Pāṭaliputra, his servants informed him:

Thereupon, Aśoka said:

Moreover, wicked ministers are treating us with contempt,
yet he has been ushered into Takṣaśilā with great honor.
In this manner, Aśoka was led into the kingdom of the Khaśas in detail;
two great *mahānagnas* took refuge with him,
and he provided them with a share of his livelihood.

the deities said:
"Aśoka shall become a universal monarch with a fourfold army."
