he listens to the true Dharma and performs services for the Saṅgha.
He went to the Kukkuṭārāma monastery.
There, an elder named Yaśas, an arhat endowed with the six superknowledges,
sat before him to listen to the Dharma.
And the Elder began to look at him;
he saw that Vītaśoka had accumulated the necessary causes and was in his final existence, such that he was to attain arhatship in that very body.
Therefore, the Elder spoke in praise of the going forth.
Upon hearing this, a longing arose in him:
"May I go forth into homelessness under the teaching of the Blessed One.
Then, rising up with palms joined in reverence, he said to the Elder:
"May I receive the going-forth and the full ordination in the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya; may I attain the state of a monk and practice the holy life under your guidance.
The Elder said, "Child,"
"Give leave to King Aśoka.
Then Vītaśoka approached King Aśoka and, with palms joined in reverence, said:
"Your Majesty, grant me your permission."
"I shall go forth from the home to the homeless state with perfect faith in the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya. And he said:
"I was like a wild elephant, unrestrained and wandering in delusion; now, by the goad of your wisdom and through the Buddha's instructions according to the rule, I have been turned back."
But you ought to grant me one boon, O Lord of Kings: may I bear the auspicious emblem of the supreme teaching of the Lokāloka, the most excellent of worlds.
And having heard this, the king, his throat choked with tears, embraced Vītaśoka around the neck and said:
"Vītaśoka, enough of this resolve!"
Indeed, this renunciation has been undertaken by one who is discolored: dwelling in a dusty rag-robe,
wearing a garment cast off by others, and taking food as alms from the houses of strangers.
The bedding is at the foot of a tree, a layer of grass, or a layer of leaves; moreover, when afflicted by illness, medicine is indeed difficult to obtain,
and the food is butts of grain.
"And you are delicate, unable to endure the sufferings of cold, heat, hunger, and thirst.
Be gracious and turn back your mind.
Vītaśoka said: "O King!"

It is not that I do not know it; nor am I one who craves sense objects, nor am I one overcome by exhaustion; I do not desire to attain the wandering life out of fear of enemies, nor am I one made wretched by noble ones.
Seeing this world afflicted by suffering, led toward death, and overwhelmed by calamity,
I, fearing birth, have resolved to go upon the auspicious and fearless path.
Upon hearing this, King Aśoka began to weep aloud.
Then Vītaśoka, seeking to console the king, said:
"O Lord, when the fall of living beings is certain once they have mounted the swaying swing of saṃsāra,"
Why do you undergo this transformation when there is a separation from everything, in every respect?
The king said, "Vītaśoka,
let practice first be undertaken in alms-gathering.
A bed of grass was spread for him in the royal park.
Food was given to him,
and he wandered through the inner apartments, obtaining costly food. Then the king said to the women of the inner apartments:
"Give him food that is suitable for one who has gone forth.
Accordingly, he obtained some spoiled, putrid beans;
and he began to consume them.
Having seen him, King Aśoka stopped him;
he was then permitted to go forth, but [the king said], "Once you have gone forth, you shall demonstrate [your realization]."
When he had gone as far as the Kukkuṭārāma,
the thought occurred to him:
"If I go forth here, I will become crowded."
Then, having gone to the Videha country, he went forth as a monk. Thereupon, by applying himself with diligence, he attained the state of Arhatship.
Then, to the Venerable Vītaśoka, who had attained Arhatship and was experiencing the joy and bliss of liberation, this thought occurred:
"Indeed, my brother wishes to see me; therefore, he set out for Pāṭaliputra and previously arrived at the gate of King Aśoka's palace."
Then he said to the doorkeeper:
"Go and inform King Aśoka that Vītaśoka is standing at the gate, desiring to see Your Majesty. Thereupon, the doorkeeper approached King Aśoka and spoke.
"Your Majesty, by good fortune, Vṛddhi-vītaśoka has arrived and stands at the gate, desiring to see Your Majesty. Thereupon the king said,
"Go quickly and let him enter."
When Vītaśoka had entered the royal palace, King Aśoka saw him and rose from his lion-throne; like a tree cut at its roots, he fell prostrate upon the ground with his whole body.
Then, gazing at the venerable Vītaśoka while weeping, he said:

I suspect that one who has attained the force of discernment and is satiated with the essence of wisdom— which is more exquisite than any other taste— does not undergo transformation even upon constantly seeing me amidst beings who are subject to worldly contact.

(A-av 65) Now, King Aśoka had a chief minister named Rādhagupta. He saw that the Venerable Vītaśoka’s robe was made of discarded rags, his bowl was made of clay, and even his food and drink were coarse and simple.
Having seen him, he prostrated at the king’s feet and, with palms joined in reverence, said:
“Your Majesty, since this man is of few desires and contented, he will certainly have accomplished his purpose;
let joy arise. Why? Because—”
For one whose food is alms, whose robe is made of rags from dust-heaps,
and whose dwelling is at the foot of a tree— how indeed could his life be anything but unsettled?
For one whose mind is vast and free from outflows, whose body is healthy and well-nourished,
and whose means of livelihood are according to his own will— his life in the world of men is a constant festival.
Having heard this, the king, with a joyful mind, said:
"Having abandoned the Mauryan lineage, the city of Magadha, and the entire collection of jewels,
and having seen the multitude of subjects whose pride, conceit, delusion, and aggression have been utterly destroyed."
I consider both your home and this city to be as if purified by glory, being exceedingly exalted;
therefore, may you indeed embrace the sublime teaching of the Holder of the Ten Powers.
Then King Aśoka, having embraced him with his whole body, seated him upon a prepared seat;
and with exquisite food, he personally gratified him by hand.
When he had finished eating—
Having understood this, he washed his hands, set aside his bowl, and sat down before the Venerable Vītaśoka to listen to the Dharma.
Then the Venerable Vītaśoka, instructing King Aśoka with a discourse on the Dharma, said:
"O King, having accomplished the sovereignty of kingship through heedfulness, may you proceed [in the Dharma]."
O King, constantly worship the three jewels, which are so difficult to find.
Having gladdened him with a discourse on the Dharma, he set out.
Then King Aśoka, with palms joined in reverence, surrounded by five hundred ministers and attended by many thousands of citizens, followed after the Venerable Vītaśoka, placing him at his head;
for it will be said:
The elder brother is indeed followed with reverence by the king;
this is truly the praiseworthy, visible fruit of the life of renunciation.
Then the venerable Vītaśoka, manifesting his own spiritual qualities before the entire multitude of people, rose into the air by means of his supernatural power and departed.

Thereupon, King Aśoka, with palms joined in reverence, surrounded and escorted by hundreds of thousands of living beings, gazed up at the expanse of the sky and, watching the venerable Vītaśoka, said:
"Free from attachment even to the affection for your own kin, you go like a bird."
As if rejecting us, who are bound by the fetters of passionate attachment.
This is the fruit of meditation for one who is self-dependent, tranquil, and moves according to the conventions of the mind; it is not seen by those blinded by passion.
Moreover,
those who were arrogant with pride have indeed been intimidated by our supreme supernatural power (*ṛddhi*);
and those whose pride in wisdom had arisen have indeed been made to bow their heads by our intelligence (*buddhi*).

Our intellects and minds, blinded regarding the fruit by the attainment of worldly objects, have been stirred to spiritual urgency; thus, with our faces clouded by tears, we have been briefly set free in this place.
There, the Venerable Vītaśoka had gone to the border regions for lodging and food,
and a severe illness arose in him. Upon hearing this, King Aśoka dispatched medicines and attendants.
When he was touched by that disease, his head became bald;
and when the disease had departed, hair grew back upon his head. He then dismissed both the physician and the attendants.
And he generally subsisted on cow’s milk as his food.
Having gone to a cowherd settlement, he wandered about for alms.
At that time, in the city of Puṇḍravardhana, a lay follower of the Nirgranthas had a painted image of the Buddha placed at the feet of a Nirgrantha.
The lay follower informed King Aśoka,
and having heard this, the king said, "Let him be brought here quickly."
Above him, for one yojana, the yakṣas hear it; below him, for one yojana, the nāgas hear it.
Thus, in that very instant, he was brought by the yakṣas.
Upon seeing this, the enraged king declared,
"All Ājīvikas in Puṇḍravardhana are to be executed!
Eventually, on a single day, eighteen thousand Ājīvikas were put to death.
Then, in Pāṭaliputra, another lay follower of the Nirgranthas had a painted image of the Buddha placed at the feet of the Nirgrantha.
Upon hearing this, the enraged king had that lay follower of the Nirgranthas, along with his circle of kinsmen, brought into his house and burned with fire.
He also issued a command: "To whoever gives me the head of the Nirgrantha, I shall give a dīnāra."
Thus it was proclaimed.
And that venerable Vītaśoka arrived to spend the night in the house of an Ābhīra;
he was afflicted by disease, his robes were coarse, and his hair, nails, and beard were long.
The thought occurred to the Ābhīrī woman: "This Nirgrantha has come to our house for the night's lodging.
She said to her husband:
"Noble son, this dīnāra of ours has been successfully obtained."
"Having slain this Nirgrantha, I shall bring his head to King Aśoka.
Then that Ābhīra drew his sword and approached the Venerable Vītaśoka.
Thereupon, the Venerable Vītaśoka projected his knowledge of the past.
He saw that this fruit of his own past actions had now arrived;
therefore, relying solely on karma, he remained steadfast.
Then, by that cowherd, his head was severed.
"It has been brought to King Aśoka;
give him a dīnāra."
When King Aśoka saw him, he did not recognize him;
moreover, the hairs on his head were sparse and did not appear distinct.
Thereupon, physicians and attendants were brought.
Having seen it, they said,
"Your Majesty, this is the head of Vītaśoka.
Upon hearing this, the king fainted and fell to the ground.
After pouring water over it, he set it down.
Then the ministers said,
"Your Majesty, even those who are free from passion have experienced pain here."
"Let the gift of fearlessness be granted to all sentient beings! Thus, once the king had granted the gift of fearlessness,
no one was to be executed again.

Then the monks, overcome with doubt, questioned the Venerable Upagupta, the dispeller of all doubts: "Venerable One, what karma was performed by the Venerable Vītaśoka, the ripening of which resulted in his being slain by a weapon?
The Elder replied:
"Indeed, venerable ones, actions were performed by him in former births. Listen!
Once upon a time, monks, in the past, a certain hunter made his living by killing deer. In a forest, there was a well."
Having gone there, that hunter, being greedy, set out snares and traps and slaughtered the deer.
When Buddhas do not appear in the world, Pratyekabuddhas arise;
[the rest is] as explained at length.
A certain pratyekabuddha, having finished his meal at that well, emerged from it and sat cross-legged at the foot of a tree.
Because of his fragrance, the deer did not come to that well.
The hunter arrived and saw that the deer had not come to the well;
following their tracks, he came upon the Pratyekabuddha.
Upon seeing him, a thought arose in his mind.
By him this calamity was brought about;
therefore, having drawn his sword from its scabbard, he killed that Pratyekabuddha.
What do you think, venerable ones?
This very hunter is Vitaśoka.
Because of the ripening of that karma by which he slaughtered deer, a great disease arose.

Because of the ripening of that karma by which he slaughtered a Pratyekabuddha with a weapon, after experiencing suffering in the hells for many thousands of years, he was reborn among humans for five hundred births.
He was slain by a weapon;
due to the remainder of that karma, even though he has now attained arhatship, he is again slain by a weapon.
What karma did he perform by which he was reborn into a high-born family?
And he attained arhatship.
The Elder said:
"I went forth under Kāśyapa, the Perfectly Enlightened One."
He became one who delighted in giving.
Consequently, he caused donors and patrons to provide meals for the Saṅgha;
he had refreshments, drinks of gruel, and invitations prepared, and he offered parasols at the stūpas.
He performed acts of worship with a collection of banners, flags, perfumes, garlands, flowers, and musical instruments.
As the ripening of that karma, he was reborn into a high family.
Having practiced celibacy for ten thousand years, he made a perfect vow.
"By the ripening of that karma, he attained arhatship.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, the Vītaśoka-avadāna, in the glorious Divyāvadāna.
In the *Kuṇālāvadāna*,
there is the narrative of the minister Yaśas;
he, having recently conceived faith in the Buddha's teaching, was at that place where he saw the followers of the Śākyaputra.
Whether in a crowded place or in private, he would prostrate with his head at the king's feet and pay him homage.
Now, there was a minister of his named Yaśas who was supremely devoted to the Blessed One;
he said to the king:
"Your Majesty, you ought not to perform prostrations before those who have gone forth from all four castes;
for there are Śākya novices who have gone forth from all four castes.
To him, the king said nothing at all.
Then, after some time, that king said to all his ministers:
"A requirement must be met with the heads of various living beings;
you must bring the head of such-and-such a creature, and you [another] the head of such-and-such."
The minister Yaśas was commanded again, "Bring a human head. When the heads had been brought, he said to them,
"Go and sell these heads for their price."
Then all the heads had been sold, yet no one would take that very human head. Thereupon, the king said:

"Give this head to someone even without a price," he said; yet, no one appeared who would accept it. Then, failing to find anyone to take the head, the minister Yaśas approached the king with shame and spoke these words.
"O King, the heads of oxen, donkeys, camels, deer, and birds were taken by men for their prices;
but this human head is not considered praiseworthy, and thus it is not accepted even without a price."
Then the king said to that minister, "What is this?
[The minister replied,] "This human head; no one will take it."
The minister said,
"Because of its loathsomeness.
The king replied:
"Is it only this head that is loathsome, or are all human heads so?
The minister replied,
"All human heads are so."
The king said, "What is this? Is even my own head loathsome? And he, out of fear, did not wish to speak the truth of the matter.
He was addressed by the king:
"Minister, let the truth be told. He replied: "So be it."
Then that king, having established the minister in his promise and rejecting this matter,
said: "O sir, you who are bewildered by the intoxication born of beauty and power,
this is not fitting for you, since you wish to dissuade me from prostrating at the feet of a mendicant."
Even without a price, because it is loathsome, there is no recipient for it on earth;
yet, if merit has been earned here by me having obtained this head, what is wrong in that?
You perceive birth among the Śākya monks, yet you do not perceive the virtues within them;
therefore, out of the intoxication and arrogance of birth, you harm yourself and others through delusion.
At the time of bringing home a bride, or at the time of marriage, there is an examination of birth, but not at the time of dharma;
for in the performance of dharma, virtuous qualities are the cause, and virtuous qualities do not take birth into consideration.
If faults found in those of high birth incur censure in this world,
how is it that virtues found in low-born people do not deserve honor?
For by the power of the mind, the body of men is either reviled or honored;
therefore, I honor the Śākyas because their minds are pure, like those of the Śākya ascetics.
If a twice-born man devoid of virtues is held in contempt even if he is renowned as fallen,
then surely a person born of a low family who is endowed with auspicious qualities is worthy of salutation and honor.
Moreover,
have you not heard these words of that compassionate bull among the Śākyas: "The wise are able to extract the essence from what is essence-less, even from these machines"?
If I desire to carry out that command of yours who speak nothing but the truth, yet you strive to obstruct it, this is not the mark of a friend.
When my body, like a crushed stalk of sugarcane, lies abandoned upon the earth— incapable of rising, bowing, joining palms in salutation,
or performing any laborious task— what wholesome deed will I then be able to accomplish with this body?
Therefore, it is fitting for me to extract the essence from this body before its end at the cremation ground.
Those who do not perceive the essence within the body— which is like a house set ablaze or like a treasure-trove submerged in water— until its destruction and end; (A-av 74) [they are lost].
Not perceiving the essential, those who are unwise and lack skill regarding what is essential and what is not,
despair at the time of entering the mouth of the makara of death.
It is better that a jar of cream, its essence extracted, be broken after the consumption of curd, ghee, butter, milk, and buttermilk; for it does not cause much reproach. Just so is the body.
At the time of death, grief does not reach one whose essence has been carried away by good conduct.
But when death here forcibly shatters the jar of the body of those who are averse to good conduct and are arrogant,
then the fire of grief burns their hearts.
Like a jar of curd that has been broken and from which all its essence has been extracted.
Therefore, you ought not to create an obstacle for me regarding this prostration of the body;
for one who, shrouded in the darkness of delusion, reckons "I am superior" without investigation, is a fool.
But the wise man investigates the body by means of the lamps of the teachings of the One Possessing Ten Powers.
He does not perceive any difference in the body between a king and a servant.
For the constituent elements of skin, flesh, bone, sinews, and so forth are indeed the same for all men; it is only by means of external ornaments that the excellence of the body is produced.
But that which is desired here as the essence is that which, depending upon this wretched body, [is cultivated].
"Virtuous acts such as rising to greet and paying homage are instigated by the wise.
Thus ends the narrative of King Aśoka.
Then King Aśoka, having realized that the body is more insubstantial even than balls of water, sand, or pieces of castor-oil wood,
and having established for many eons the fruit arising from prostrations and other such acts as being more substantial than Mount Sumeru or the great earth, [honored] the Blessed One.

Desiring to adorn himself for the worship of the stūpa, he went to the Kukkuṭārāma surrounded by his retinue of ministers; standing there at the end of the assembly of elders with palms joined in reverence, he said:
"Is there anyone else who has been designated by the All-Seeing One, just as I was designated by that wise one through the gift of dust?"

Thereupon, the Elder of the Saṅgha named Yaśas said: "It was so, Great King. At the time of the Blessed One’s final nirvāṇa, having subdued the nāga Apalāla and [the nāgas] Kumbhakarṇī, Caṇḍālī, Gopālī, and [the nāga] Mathura, he arrived at Mathurā."
Thereupon the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
"Ānanda, in this city of Mathurā, one hundred years after the Tathāgata has passed into parinirvāṇa, there will be a perfumer named Gupta.

He will have a son named Upagupta, the foremost of those who give instruction—a Buddha without the marks—who, after I have passed into parinirvāṇa for one hundred years, will perform the work of a Buddha."
"Do you see, Ānanda, that dark-blue line of clouds in the distance?
"I do, Venerable Sir.
"Ānanda, this is the mountain named Urumuṇḍa; here, one hundred years after the Tathāgata has attained final nirvāṇa, there will be a forest hermitage named Naṭabhaṭikā."
"Ānanda, among all resting places conducive to tranquility (*śamatha*), this will be the foremost for me, namely the forest hermitage called Naṭabhaṭikā. And he said:
"The most excellent of instructors is the highly renowned Upagupta."
The Lord of the World has prophesied that he will perform the work of a Buddha.
The king asked:
"Has that pure being already been reborn,
or has he not yet been reborn even now?"
The Elder said:

"That Great-souled One was born on Mount Urumuṇḍa; having conquered the afflictions, he dwells there surrounded by a host of Arhats for the sake of compassion toward the world. Moreover, O King, that Pure Being, who sports like the Omniscient One, proclaims the sublime Dharma before his assembly."
He is the one who leads by the thousands the gods, asuras, lords of serpents, and humans to the city of liberation.
At that time, the Venerable Upagupta was dwelling in the Naṭabhaṭika forest hermitage, surrounded by eighteen thousand arhats.
Having heard this, he summoned the king and his circle of ministers and said:
"Prepare the body of elephants, chariots, and cavalry; I shall depart quickly for Mount Urumuṇḍa."
I shall behold the noble Upagupta, an Arhat who has directly realized the liberation from all outflows.
Then he was addressed by the ministers:
"Your Majesty, a messenger should be sent; that resident of the realm will come to Your Majesty of his own accord. The king said:
He does not deserve to come to us; rather, we alone ought to go to him. Moreover, I believe his body is made of diamond, even more massive than a mountain.
For that man who would disregard the command of Upagupta, who is equal to the Teacher himself.
When the king sent a messenger to the presence of the Elder Upagupta with the message that he would come to see the Elder,
the Elder Upagupta thought:
"If the king comes, there will be distress for the great multitude of people."
And regarding the range of his activity,
the Elder then declared:
"I shall come myself."
Then, for the sake of the Elder Upagupta, the king had a ferry established between Mathurā and Pāṭaliputra so that he might travel by boat.
Thereupon, the Elder Upagupta, out of favor toward King Aśoka, boarded a boat surrounded by eighteen thousand arhats and arrived at Pāṭaliputra.
Then, the king’s men informed King Aśoka.
"Your Majesty, by good fortune you prosper!
For the sake of showing you favor, this Citteśvara, together with Sopagupta—the helmsman of the teaching who has crossed to the further shore of the flood of existence—has arrived on foot before you.
Upon hearing this, the king, with a joyful mind, removed from his own body a pearl necklace worth a hundred thousand pieces and gave it to the messenger of the pleasant news.
He summoned the bell-ringer and said to him, "Let the bells be sounded throughout Pāṭaliputra; let it be announced that the Elder Upagupta is arriving. It should be said:"

He who, having cast aside poverty— the root of misfortune— desires here in this world abundant splendor and glory, and who seeks the cause for heaven and liberation, let him behold the compassionate Upagupta.

Those who have not seen the foremost of bipeds, the Teacher, the Greatly Compassionate One, the Self-Existent, behold the Elder Upagupta, who is like the Teacher himself, sublime, and a lamp for the three realms of existence.

When the king had caused a bell to be rung in Pāṭaliputra and the city to be adorned, he traveled two and a half yojanas with all musical instruments, all flowers, perfumes, and garlands, accompanied by all the citizens and all his ministers, to go out and meet the Elder Upagupta.
The king saw the Elder Upagupta from afar, surrounded by eighteen thousand arhats in a crescent-shaped formation.

As soon as the king beheld the Elder Upagupta, he descended from the back of his elephant and approached the riverbank on foot; placing one foot upon the riverbank and the second upon a wooden plank in the boat, he [stood] before the Elder Upagupta.
Having embraced him with his entire body, he helped him out of the boat.

Once he had helped him out, like a tree cut down at its roots, he prostrated himself with his whole body at the feet of Upagupta; then, having rubbed the feet with his face, he rose, knelt with both knees upon the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, gazing at the Elder Upagupta, he said:

When I had slain the hosts of my enemies and obtained the earth— adorned by the oceans and its mountains, ruled under a single umbrella— that joy was not as great as the joy I feel now upon beholding you, O Elder.
Upon seeing you, O Lord of the excellent teaching, a twofold clarity of faith arises within me here;
and through the very sight of you, another, pure, incomparable Self-Become One has been seen by me today.
Moreover:
When the compassionate Lord of Jinas has entered into peace, you perform the work of a Buddha throughout the three worlds;
when the one who blinds the world with delusion has perished, you, like the sun, are the creator of the radiance of wisdom.

O Lord, you who are like a Teacher, the sole eye of the world, the most excellent among instructors, and the worthy refuge—tell me quickly today your command; O Being of Pure Essence, I shall carry out your word.
Then the Elder Upagupta, stroking the king’s head with his right hand, said:
“O King, having attained royal sovereignty through heedfulness, may you proceed [in the Dharma];
O Ruler, constantly worship the Three Jewels, which are so difficult to find.”

Moreover, Great King, that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One—the supreme charioteer of beings—has entrusted his teaching to you and me in the midst of the assembly; it must be guarded and preserved by us with great effort. The king said:
"Elder, I shall carry out exactly what has been instructed by the Blessed One. Why?

Because my earth has been adorned on all sides with various stupas resembling mountain peaks, with raised parasols and banners variegated with jewels, and the repositories of relics have been made extensive."
Moreover:
"The self, son, home, wife, and even the earth and the treasury— "
In the teaching of the Dharma King, nothing whatsoever has been left unrenounced.
The Elder Upagupta said:
"Excellent, excellent, Great King! This very thing should be practiced. Why? Because:"
Those who live by the Dharma through their bodies, their enjoyments, and their very lives do not grieve when time has passed; they go to the beloved abode of the gods.
Then the king, with a great display of royal splendor, had the Elder Upagupta enter the palace; taking hold of him with all his limbs, he seated him upon a prepared throne.
The body of the Elder Upagupta was soft, exceedingly soft, just like a tuft of cotton or a tuft of silk-cotton.

Then the king, having experienced the touch of the Elder Upagupta’s body, spoke with palms joined in reverence: "O noble being, your limbs are soft; your body is like cotton-wool and like Kāśika silk. I, however, am unfortunate, my limbs harsh and rough, my body devoid of pleasant touch, and my frame coarse."
The Elder said:
"Indeed, a pleasing, most beautiful, and excellent gift was given by me to one who is without equal;
for I did not give a gift of dust as you have offered to the Tathāgata."
The king said: "O Elder, in my youth, having previously obtained this unsurpassed field, I sowed seeds of dust therein; such is the fruit that has now come to me."
Then the Elder, gladdening the king, said: "Great King,
behold the majesty of this field, wherein even dust grows."
By which you have obtained royal splendor and unsurpassed sovereignty.
Upon hearing this, the king’s eyes widened with wonder, and he summoned his ministers and said:
"I have obtained the sovereignty of a powerful universal monarch through the mere gift of some dust!
Noble sirs, who would not worship the Blessed One with great effort?"
Then the king, prostrating at the feet of the Elder Upagupta, said:
"This is my wish, O Elder: that I should honor those places where the Blessed Buddha dwelt, and that I should establish monuments there for the benefit of future generations."
The Elder said:
"Excellent, Great King! Your resolve is noble;
I shall now demonstrate it to you."
With palms joined in reverence, I bow to those lands inhabited by the Buddha;
having gone there, I shall undoubtedly visit their sacred sites.
Then the king, having equipped his fourfold army and taking with him perfumes, garlands, and flowers, set out accompanied by the Elder Upagupta.
Thereupon, the Elder Upagupta led King Aśoka into the Lumbinī grove first of all; extending his right hand, he said:
"In this place, Great King, the Blessed One was born. And he spoke further:
This is indeed the first shrine of the Buddha, the one with the supreme vision;
as soon as he was born here, that Sage took seven steps upon the earth.
Having looked in the four directions, he spoke these words of old:
"This is my final birth; this is my last dwelling in a womb."
Then the king, prostrating himself there with his whole body at the [Buddha’s] feet, rose up and, with palms joined and weeping, said:
"Blessed and meritorious are those by whom that Great Sage was seen,
and by whom his delightful words were heard when he appeared."
Then the Elder, in order to inspire faith in the king, said:
"Great King, what will you see of that deity by whom the best of speakers was seen while he was being born in this forest?"
Having heard the words of the sage as he took seven steps, [he proceeded].
The king said, "I would like to see it, O Elder.
Then the Elder Upagupta, extending his right hand toward the branch of the tree from which Queen Mahāmāyā had given birth, said:
"The resident celestial maiden who dwells here in this Aśoka tree is one who has beheld the Perfectly Awakened One."
May he manifest his own body in person for the sake of increasing King Aśoka’s favor.
When that deity had stood before the Elder Upagupta in her own form, she spoke with palms joined in reverence:
"Elder, what do you command?
Then the Elder said to King Aśoka:
"Great King, this is that very deity by whom the Blessed One was seen being born.
Then the king, with palms joined in reverence, said to that deity:
"Did you see him as he was being born, his limbs adorned with the marks of greatness, his eyes as broad as lotuses?"
You have heard those charming words of that bull among men spoken earlier in this forest.
The deity said:
"Indeed, I beheld the foremost of bipeds, golden-hued, as he was being born."
Even as he was taking his seven steps, the words of that Teacher were heard.

The king said, "Tell me, O goddess, what kind of splendor attended the Blessed One at the time of his birth? The goddess replied, "It is not possible for me to describe it fully with words; however, listen to a brief account."
The world of the three realms, including Indra, radiant with emanated forms and white as gold, was pleasing to the eyes;
and the entire earth, bounded by the oceans and filled with mountains, shook like a ship situated in the great sea.
When the king had given a hundred thousand [pieces of gold] for the birthplace and had established a caitya, he departed.
Then the Elder Upagupta, having settled the king in Kapilavastu, extended his right hand and said:
In this place, O Great King, the Bodhisattva was presented to King Śuddhodana.

Having seen him—his body adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man and his appearance so lovely as to never tire the beholder—the King prostrated himself with his entire body at the feet of the Bodhisattva.
This, O Great King, is the divine shrine named Śākyavardha.
At that time, it was thought that as soon as the Bodhisattva was born, he would be brought forward to worship the gods;
and all the deities prostrated themselves at the feet of the Bodhisattva.
Thereupon, King Śuddhodana declared, "This one is a god even for the gods," and thus he gave the Bodhisattva the name Devātideva (God of Gods).
In this place, Great King, the Bodhisattva was presented to the Brahmins, the diviners, and the astrologers;
in this place, he was prophesied by the seer Asita that he would become a Buddha in the world.
In this place, O Great King, he was raised by Mahāprajāpatī;
in this place, he was taught the knowledge of scripts;

and in this place, he became a master of riding elephants, riding horses, charioteering, the handling of arrows and bows, the grasping of javelins, the wielding of hooks, and in all the sciences befitting his lineage.
This was the Bodhisattva’s hall of exertion.

In this place, O Great King, the Bodhisattva, surrounded by hundreds of thousands of deities and together with sixty thousand women, experienced sensual pleasure. In this very place, the Bodhisattva, distressed by the sight of an old man, a sick man, and a corpse, took refuge in the forest.

Sitting in this place in the shade of a rose-apple tree, secluded from evil and unwholesome states, he attained the first dhyāna—which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, born of seclusion, and characterized by joy and bliss similar to that which is free from outflows. Then, when midday had passed and the time for the meal was over, the shadows of the other trees slanted toward the east, inclined toward the east, and sloped toward the east; yet the shadow of the rose-apple tree remained over the Bodhisattva.
He did not leave his body.
And having seen this, King Śuddhodana fell prostrate with his entire body at the feet of the Bodhisattva.
By way of this gate, the Bodhisattva, surrounded by hundreds of thousands of deities, departed from Kapilavastu at midnight.
In this place, the Bodhisattva gave his ornaments and the horse to Chandaka and sent him back. And he said:
"Chandaka, the ornaments, and the horse have been sent back here;
the Hero, without attendants, has entered the forest of asceticism alone."
In this place, the Bodhisattva, having received saffron robes from the hunter in exchange for his Kāśika garments, went forth into homelessness;
in this place, he was invited by Bhārgava to his hermitage.
In this region, the Bodhisattva was invited by King Bimbisāra to share half of the kingdom;
in this region, he approached Ārāḍa Kālāma. And it is said:
"In this grove of asceticism dwell the sages known as Udraka Ārāḍaka."
They were scorched by that lord of men, who had attained the state of a noble being.
In this place, the Bodhisattva practiced austerities for six years. And it is said:
"Having performed severe penance for six years, the Great Sage realized, 'This is not the path to higher knowledge,' and he abandoned it."
In this place, the Bodhisattva partook of sixteenfold honeyed milk-rice from the hands of Nandā and Nandabalā, the daughters of the village headman.
And it is said:
"In this place, having eaten the honeyed milk-rice of Nandā..."
The Great Hero, the best among speakers, went to the foot of the Bodhi tree.
In this place, the Bodhisattva was greeted by the Naga king Kālika as he was approaching the foot of the Bodhi tree;
and he said:
Praised by Kālikabhujagendra, the best of speakers set out upon this path toward the seat of awakening, seeking the deathless state.
Then the king, having prostrated at the feet of the elder, spoke with palms joined in reverence:
"May we also see the lord of nagas by whom the Tathāgata was seen as he proceeded along this path with the majestic stride of a rutting lord of nagas?"
Then the Naga king Kālika, standing near the Elder with palms joined in reverence, said:
"Elder, what do you command?
Thereupon, the Elder spoke to the king.
"Great King, this is that Nāga king Kālika, by whom the Blessed One was praised as he was departing for the foot of the Bodhi tree by way of this path.
Then the king, with palms joined in reverence, said to the Nāga king Kālika:
"Have you seen my Teacher, whose complexion is like blazing gold, who is without equal, and whose face is like the autumn moon?"
Tell me a single portion of the qualities of the One Possessing the Ten Powers; tell me indeed, what was the splendor of the Sugata at that time?
Kālika said:
It is not possible to describe this fully with words; however, hear it in brief.
Struck by the sole of his foot, the earth together with its mountains shook in six ways.
In the world of men, the splendor of the moon-like Sugata is more radiant than the rays of the sun; it is inexhaustible and delightful.
When the king had established the caitya and departed,
the Elder Upagupta led the king to the foot of the Bodhi tree, extended his right hand, and said:

In this place, O Great King, the Bodhisattva, accompanied by great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*), having conquered the entire host of Māra, fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. And it is said:
"Here, at the foot of the tree of awakening, the Bull among Sages swiftly shattered and cast away the forces of Namuci;
for there, that peerless person attained this nectar-like, sublime, and supreme enlightenment."
When the king had offered a hundred thousand [pieces of gold] at the site of enlightenment and established a caitya, he departed. Then,
the Elder Upagupta said to King Aśoka:
In this place, the Blessed One received four stone bowls from the Four Great Kings and joined them into a single bowl.
In this place, he also accepted almsfood from the two merchants Trapuṣa and Bhallika.
In this place, while proceeding toward Vārāṇasī, the Blessed One was praised by the Ājīvika Upaga.
When the Elder had led the king to Ṛṣipatana, he extended his right hand and said:
"In this place, Great King, the Blessed One set in motion the Wheel of Dharma—righteous, consisting of twelve aspects and three turnings. And he said:
"The auspicious wheel composed of Dharma turns back the cycle of saṃsāra."
In this region, the unsurpassed [teaching] was set in motion by the Lord.
In this place, a thousand matted-hair ascetics were ordained;
in this place, the Dharma was taught to King Bimbisāra,
and by King Bimbisāra, the Truths were realized.
In this place, the Blessed One taught the Dharma to Śakra, the lord of the gods, along with eighty-four thousand deities and many thousands of Magadhan brahmins and householders;
and Śakra, as well as those eighty-four thousand deities, perceived the truths.
In this place the Great Miracle was displayed.
In this place the Blessed One, having spent the rainy season among the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three and having taught the Dharma to his mother, descended surrounded by a host of gods.
[The narrative continues] in detail until the Elder, having led King Aśoka to Kuśinagarī, extended his right palm and said:
"In this place, O Great King, the Blessed One, having completed all the work of a Buddha, passed away into the realm of Nirvana without remainder. And it is said:

'Having disciplined the world—including its gods, humans, asuras, yakṣas, and nāgas—within the inexhaustible Dharma and Vinaya, the wise one, his mind stilled due to the absence of beings to be trained, the Great Seer of supreme compassion has gone to peace.'"

Upon hearing this, the king fainted and fell down; only after being revived by the sprinkling of water did he somehow regain consciousness. Then, having bestowed a hundred thousand [pieces of gold] upon the final nirvana and established a stupa, he prostrated at his feet and said:
"Elder, this is my wish: that I shall perform the funeral rites for the bodies of those disciples whom the Blessed One has designated as foremost.
The Elder said, "Excellent, excellent, Great King!"
"Excellent is your resolve!
Having led King Aśoka into the Jeta Grove, the Elder extended his right hand and said,
"Great King, this is the stūpa of the Elder Śāriputra."
"Let his worship be performed," [the minister said]. The king asked,
"What were his virtues?"
The Elder said:
"For he was designated by the Blessed One as the second Teacher, the commander of the army of Dharma, the turner of the wheel of Dharma, and the foremost among those possessed of wisdom."
The wisdom of all the world, with the exception of the Tathāgata’s,
does not equal even a sixteenth part of Śāriputra’s wisdom.
And it is said:
"The peerless Wheel of the True Dharma which was set in motion by the Victor was indeed followed by that wise Śāriputra."
Who else here besides the Buddha could rightly describe, without exception, that storehouse of a multitude of virtues, having understood it— other than the person Śāradvatīputra?
Then the king, with a joyful mind, having offered a hundred thousand [pieces of gold] at the stupa of the Elder Śāradvatīputra, spoke with palms joined in reverence:
"With devotion I pay homage to Śāradvatīputra, who is liberated from attachment to existence, whose fame illuminates the world, and who is the hero supreme among those possessed of wisdom."
Then the Elder Upagupta, pointing out the stūpa of the Elder Mahāmaudgalyāyana, said:
"Great King, this is the stūpa of the Elder Mahāmaudgalyāyana;
let worship be offered to it."
The king asked,
"What were his virtues?
The elder replied:

For he was designated by the Blessed One as the foremost among those possessed of supernatural powers (ṛddhimat), by whom, with his right big toe, the Vaijayanta palace of Śakra, lord of the gods, was made to tremble, and the two nāga kings Nanda and Upananda were subdued. And it is said:
"By whom the abode of Śakra was shaken with his big toe."
That Kolita, the best of the twice-born, should be honored with great effort.
Who could reach the further shore of that ocean of virtues— the one of pure intellect who has tamed those two formidable lords of serpents, so exceedingly difficult to subdue in the world?
When the king had offered a hundred thousand [pieces of gold] at the stūpa of Mahāmaudgalyāyana, he spoke with palms joined in reverence:
"He who is the foremost among those possessed of supernatural powers, liberated from birth, old age, sorrow, and suffering— "
I pay homage with my head bowed down to the renowned Maudgalyāyana.
Then the Elder Upagupta, pointing out the stūpa of the Elder Mahākāśyapa, said:
"This, Great King, is the stūpa of the Elder Mahākāśyapa;
let worship be offered to it."
The king asked, "What were his qualities? The Elder replied:
For that great-souled one was designated by the Blessed One as the foremost among those who are free from desire, contented, and speakers of the virtues of incense;
he was invited to share half of the Buddha’s seat, clothed in white robes, a receiver of the wretched and the afflicted, and a sustainer of the Teaching. And it is said:
"A noble field of merit, a receiver of the wretched and the afflicted, free from weariness."
Wearing the robe of the Omniscient One, he is wise and a sustainer of the Teaching.
What man is able to describe exhaustively the virtues of that preceptor,
the most excellent of those seated on thrones, to whom the Jina granted half his seat?

Then King Aśoka, having offered one hundred thousand [pieces of gold] at the stūpa of the Elder Mahākāśyapa, spoke with palms joined in reverence: "I pay homage indeed to the Elder Kāśyapa, who dwells in mountain caves, whose life is one of renunciation, who has turned his back on enmity, who is endowed with tranquility, and whose virtue of contentment has increased."
Then the Elder Upagupta, pointing out the stūpa of the Elder Vatkula, said:
"This, Great King, is the stūpa of the Elder Vatkula;
let worship be performed."
The king asked,
"What were his virtues?"
The Elder said:
"That Great Being was designated by the Blessed One as the foremost among those with few afflictions;
moreover, not even a single two-line verse was ever recited by him for anyone."
The king said, "Let a kārṣāpaṇa be given here.
Then the ministers addressed him.
"Your Majesty, for what reason is a single cowrie given here when all are situated as equals?
The king said, "Listen; hear my intention in this matter."
Although he removed all the darkness from that great house with the lamp of his knowledge,
because of his state of having few desires, he did not achieve for himself that benefit for sentient beings which was accomplished by others.
Being thus rejected, she fell at the feet of that very king;
meanwhile, the ministers, filled with wonder, said:
"Oh, how great is the fewness of desires in that noble-souled one!"
He remained free from desire even for this.
Then, as the Elder Upagupta was showing the stūpa of the Elder Ānanda, he said:
"This is the stūpa of the Elder Ānanda."
"Let his worship be performed," [the minister] said. The king asked,
"What were his virtues?"
The Elder said: "For he was the attendant of the Blessed One; he was the foremost among those of great learning and a master of the scriptures. And he said:
Skilled in protecting the vessel of the Sage, firm in mindfulness, fortitude, and intelligence, an ocean of sacred learning,
possessing clear and sweet speech, honored by gods and men, he was ever joyful.
Skilled in the mind of the Perfectly Awakened One, discerning in all things, a casket of virtues, praised by the Jinas, a conqueror of the battle, honored by gods and men, he is ever-blissful.
When the king had given ten million [pieces of gold] for his stūpa,
he was addressed by the ministers:
"For what reason, O King, is he worshipped more highly than all others?
The King said: "Listen to my intention. That body of the best of speakers, whose soul is dharma, was composed of dharma and was pure."
Since it was upheld by him who is named Viśoka, he is therefore especially worthy of worship.
Since the lamp of Dharma blazes today among living beings, bringing an end to the darkness of the afflictions,
he— the son of the Lord of Sugatas— is therefore especially worthy of worship because of that power.
Just as the waters of the ocean can be held by the oceans, but certainly not by a cow's footprint—
having considered that state of the Dharma through his Lord, this Elder, a master of the sūtras, was consecrated.
Then the king, having performed worship at the stūpas of the elders and prostrating at the feet of the Elder Upagupta, spoke with a joyful mind:
"Human birth has been made fruitful; that which is attained through hundreds of sacrifices, through royal sovereignty, and through unstable riches—the supreme essence has been grasped."
This world is adorned with hundreds of shrines possessing the luster of white mountain peaks;
what difficult task have we not performed for the sake of the teaching of this peerless one?
Thus [it is said].

When King [Aśoka] had paid homage to the Elder Upagupta, he departed. Subsequently, King Aśoka bestowed one hundred thousand [pieces of gold] each at the sites of the birth, the enlightenment, the turning of the wheel of Dharma, and the final nirvana.
An exceptional faith arose in him toward that awakening, thinking, "In this world, the Blessed One has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
He sent to the Bodhi tree those jewels endowed with special qualities.
Now, King Aśoka had a chief queen named Tiṣyarakṣitā.
The thought occurred to her:
"This king is enjoying pleasure with me and is sending specially excellent jewels for the sake of enlightenment.
She then addressed Mātaṅgī.
"Are you able to kill my co-wife, Bodhi? She replied,
"I am able, but give me kārṣāpaṇa coins."
When the Mātaṅgī woman had consecrated the Bodhi tree with mantras and tied a thread around it,
the Bodhi tree began to wither;
thereupon, the king’s men reported this to the king.
"O Lord, the Bodhi tree is withering! And he said:
"O King of Men, that Bodhi tree, beneath which the Tathāgata sat and awakened to this entire world as it truly is, and attained omniscience—that very tree is now approaching its end."
Upon hearing this, the king fainted and fell to the ground;
only after water was sprinkled on him was he raised up. Then, having somehow regained consciousness, the king spoke while weeping:
"Having now seen that foot of the King of Trees, I know that today I have seen the Self-Existent One;
for once the Lord has gone to his destruction beneath the tree, my own life-breaths will also go to their destruction."
Then Tiṣyarakṣitā, seeing the king afflicted with grief, said:
"Your Majesty, if Awakening is not to be attained, I shall produce delight for Your Majesty.
The king said:
It was not a woman, but rather the Bodhi tree,
at which the Blessed One attained unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Tiṣyarakṣitā then spoke to Mātaṅgī:
"Are you able to restore the Bodhi tree to its former state?
Mātaṅgī replied,
"If even a single living being remains."
"I shall restore it to its former state.
[The story continues] in detail until, having removed the bark from the tree, she dug around its base and fed it a thousand jars of milk every day;
in a few days, it became as it was before.
Then the king’s men reported to the king:
"Your Majesty, by good fortune you prosper! He has become just as he was before."
Having heard this, his mind filled with joy, he gazed upon the Bodhi tree and said:
"That supreme double honor which was not performed by the lords of kings, such as Bimbisāra and Dyutindhara, I shall now perform."
I shall bathe the Bodhi tree with jars filled with scented water,
and I shall perform the Pañcavārṣika festival in honor of the Saṅgha.
Then the king, having filled a thousand jars made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal with scented water,

having prepared abundant food and drink, and having gathered a collection of perfumes, garlands, and flowers, bathed, put on new, long-fringed garments of fine cloth, observed the fast endowed with the eight limbs, and took up a censer of incense—
Having ascended to the roof of the palace,
he began to call out in the four directions:
"May those who are disciples of the Blessed Buddha come to show me favor!"
Moreover:
Those who have gone rightly, the disciples of the Sugata, whose senses are stilled and who have conquered the faults of desire—
worthy of honor and worshipped by men and gods, may they come here out of compassion for me.
The sons of the Sugata, the Dharma-kings, who delight in tranquility and self-restraint, who are liberated from attachments,
who are honored by asuras, gods, and humans, and whose conduct is noble— may they come here out of compassion for me.

Those noble ones who dwell in the most beautiful city of Kāśmīra, those wise ones who are in this Tamasāvana forest, and those Āryas who are on Mount Revataka in the great forest— they have all come here for the sake of showing me favor.

Those sons of the Conqueror who dwell in Lake Anavatapta, in mountain rivers, and in mountain caves— may they, who are ever devoted to meditation and possess the power of compassion, arise here today.
May those sons of the best of speakers, who dwell in the preeminent Śairīṣaka celestial palace,
come here free from sorrow, their hearts imbued with compassion, for the sake of showing me favor.
And those of great majesty who dwell on Mount Gandhamādana—
having been invited, let them come here, having generated compassion.
When the king had spoken thus, three hundred thousand monks assembled;
among them, one hundred thousand were arhats, two hundred thousand were those in training (*śaikṣa*), and the remainder were virtuous ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana-kalyāṇaka*).
No one at all was taking the seat of honor. The king asked,
"For what reason is that seat of honor not being taken?"
There, an elder named Yaśas, who possessed the six superknowledges, said:
"Great King, that seat belongs to the elder."
The king said, "Venerable sir, is there anyone else more venerable than you? The elder replied:
"O Great King, there is one designated by the Best of Speakers, the Self-controlled One who roars like a lion, as the foremost among those named Siṃhanādin:
this is the preeminent seat for Piṇḍola Bharadvāja, O Ruler."
Then the king, his hair standing on end like a kadamba flower, said:
"Is there any monk who has seen the Buddha who might be brought here?
The Elder replied:
"Great King, there is one named Piṇḍolabharadvāja who dwells as a seer of the Buddha.
The king said,
"Elder, is it possible for us to see him?"
The Elder said:
"Great King, you shall see him now;
this is the time for his arrival."
Then the king, filled with joy, said:
"A supreme and incomparable gain is mine here, as well as this unsurpassed great happiness,
since I behold that noble being in person, bearing the name of the lineage of Bharadvāja."
Then the king, with palms joined in reverence, stood gazing fixedly at the expanse of the sky.
Thereupon, the Elder Piṇḍola Bharadvāja, surrounded by many thousands of Arhats in the shape of a half-moon, descended from the sky like a royal swan and sat down at the end of the row of elders.
Upon seeing the Elder Piṇḍola Bharadvāja, those many hundreds of thousands of monks gathered around him.

King [Bimbisāra] beheld Piṇḍola Bharadvāja, with his head white with grey hair, his eyebrows hanging down over his forehead, and his pupils deeply sunken—possessing the physical form of a Pratyekabuddha.
Having seen him, the king fell at the feet of the Elder Piṇḍola Bharadvāja with his entire body, like a tree cut down at its roots.

Having wiped his feet with the tip of his mouth and risen, he placed both his knees upon the surface of the earth and, with palms joined in reverence, gazing at the Elder Piṇḍola-Bharadvāja while weeping, he said:

"When I had slain the hosts of my enemies and obtained the earth— with its oceans as ornaments and its mountains— under a single umbrella, even then I felt no such joy as that which I feel now upon beholding you, O Elder."
"By seeing you, the Tathāgata has been seen by me today.

From obtaining [the opportunity for] compassion and from seeing you, a twofold clarity of faith has arisen within me. Moreover, O Elder, my Teacher, the Blessed Buddha, the Lord of the Three Worlds, has been seen by you."
Then the Elder Piṇḍola Bharadvāja, raising his eyebrows with both hands and gazing at King Aśoka, said:
"Indeed, I have seen many times that peerless Great Seer,
whose splendor is equal to molten gold."
Bearing the thirty-two marks, with a face like the autumn moon, possessing a voice superior to that of Brahmā, he indeed dwells in the state of passionlessness.
The king asked, "Elder, where did you see the Blessed One, and how?
The elder replied:

"Great King, when the Blessed One, having conquered the host of Māra, first spent the rainy season retreat at Rājagṛha together with five hundred arhats, I was there at that very time. I beheld that one worthy of offerings with perfect vision. And he said:
"The Great Sage, free from passion, was surrounded by those free from passion."
When that Tathāgata had spent the rainy season retreat in Rājagṛha.
At that time, I was there in the presence of Subuddha;
just as you see me now before your eyes, so too did I behold the Sage.

Furthermore, Great King, when the Blessed One performed the Great Miracle at Śrāvastī for the sake of defeating the non-Buddhist teachers, manifesting a vast array of Buddha-ornaments reaching as far as the Akaniṣṭha heaven— at that time,
I was right there. I thought,
"This display of the Buddha's power is difficult to endure."
And it is said:
"O King, when the heretics who had set out upon a wrong path were indeed subdued by the Blessed One through the method of his miraculous power,
I then witnessed that magnificent display of the One Possessing the Ten Powers, which brought joy to all living beings."

Furthermore, Great King, when the Blessed One, having spent the rains retreat among the Trāyastriṃśa gods and taught the Dharma to his mother, descended to the city of Sāṃkāśya surrounded by a host of gods, I was present right there at that time. I witnessed that excellence of gods and humans, and the excellence of a universal monarch manifested by Utpalavarṇā.
When the best of speakers, having descended from the world of the gods after spending the rains retreat there,
was present even there, I beheld that sage, the supreme being.

Great King, when I was invited by Sumāgadhā, the daughter of Anāthapiṇḍada, and went to Puṇḍravardhana with five hundred arhats by means of my supernormal power, I then took hold of a mountain crag with my supernormal power, ascended into the expanse of the sky, and went to Puṇḍravardhana.
And for your sake, an injunction was issued to me by the Blessed One:
"You must not enter final nirvana until the Dharma has disappeared. And he said:
"When the Leader, the Guru, went by the power of his supernatural faculties, having been invited to Sumāgadhā..."
Then, having gained strength through his supernatural power, he indeed went swiftly to Mount Puṇḍravardhana.
Then that compassionate one, born of the Śākya clan, gave me this command:
"Nirvāṇa must not be attained by me until this Dharma has disappeared."

Furthermore, Great King, when formerly in your childhood you threw a handful of dust into the bowl of the Blessed One— who had entered Rājagṛha for alms— with the thought, "I shall give him flour-meal," and Rādhagupta expressed his approval,
the Blessed One declared of you: "This boy, after I have passed into final nirvāṇa a hundred years, will be Aśoka in the city of Pāṭaliputra."

"There shall be a king named Nāma, a righteous wheel-turning monarch of one quarter of the earth, who will cause my relics to be widely distributed and will establish eighty-four thousand stūpas for the King of Dharma; at that time, I shall be right there. And he said:
When you offered a handful of dust into the bowl of the Buddha out of childish devotion, I was right there at that very moment.
The king said, "Elder,
where will you stay now?"
The Elder said:
"O King, I dwell there on Mount Gandhamādana, the king of mountains to the north, together with my fellow students."
The king asked, "How large is the Elder's retinue?
The Elder replied,
"O best of men, his retinue consists of sixty thousand Arhats."
I dwell together with those who are free from desire and have conquered all defilement.
Moreover, Great King, what is the use of this doubt?
Let the community of monks be served.
Once the community of monks has finished eating, I shall offer them my greetings.
The king said, "So be it, as the Elder commands. However,
awakened by the recollection of the Buddha, I shall first perform the ritual bathing of the Bodhi tree."
"And immediately thereafter, I shall attend upon the community of monks with pleasing food.
Then King Sarvamitra addressed the announcer:
"I shall give a hundred thousand [pieces of gold] to the noble Saṅgha."
"I shall bathe the Bodhi tree with a thousand jars;
let it be proclaimed in my name that there is a five-year festival.
At that time, Kunāla's two eyes were still unimpaired.
He stood at the king’s right side;
he raised two fingers but did not speak a word, signaling by his gesture:
"I shall give you double."
As soon as Kunāla had placed it in his hand, the entire multitude of people burst into laughter.
Then the king, having also laughed, said:
"Aha! Rādhagupta, by whom was this raised?"
Rādhagupta replied,

At a later time, he went to the Himalayas.
There, he discovered five hundred deer who had entered a single cave after being struck by lightning;
he captured them all with a snare.
The thought occurred to him:
"If I kill it, the meat will become putrid.
Therefore, he plucked out the eyes of five hundred deer.
With their eyes plucked out, they did not flee anywhere;
in this way, the eyes of many hundreds of deer were torn out. What do you think, venerable ones?
That hunter was this very Kunāla.

Because he plucked out the eyes of many hundreds of deer there, as the ripening of that karma, he experienced suffering in the hells for many hundreds of thousands of years; thereafter, due to the specific nature of that karma, for five hundred births...
His eyes were plucked out. What karma did he perform, the ripening of which caused him to be reborn on a high social level and become so handsome?
And the vision of the Truth has been accomplished.
Therefore, venerable ones, listen:
in the past, in a time gone by, when the lifespan of beings was forty thousand years, a Perfectly Enlightened One named Krakucchanda appeared in the world.
When the Perfectly Awakened One Krakucchanda, having completed all the work of a Buddha, passed away into the realm of Nirvana without remainder,
King Aśoka caused a stupa made of the four jewels to be built for him.
When King Aśoka had passed away and a king lacking faith was established in the kingdom, [the following occurred].
Those jewels were carried off by those who take what is not given;
only dust and wood remained.
When the multitude of people went there and saw that it was ruined, they began to grieve.
And at that time, a certain son of a guild-president was there;
he said to him:
"Why are you weeping? they were asked. They replied, "The stupa of the Perfectly Awakened One Krakucchanda was composed of the four precious gems; it has now fallen into ruin."
Then, he restored the dilapidated image of the Perfectly Awakened One Krakucchanda that was there, having made it equal in size to his body,
and he made this perfect vow:
"May I please a Teacher exactly like the Teacher Krakucchanda."
"May I not cause him to become disenchanted.
What do you think, venerable ones?
That son of a merchant was none other than this Kunāla.
Because he constructed a stūpa for Krakucchanda, through the ripening of that karma, he was reborn into a high-ranking family.
Because he constructed an image, through the ripening of that karma, Kunāla became handsome and pleasing.
Because he made a formal aspiration, through the ripening of that karma, Kunāla pleased a Teacher exactly like Śākyamuni, the Perfectly Awakened One, and did not displease him.
And the vision of the Truth was attained.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, the Kunālāvadāna, in the glorious Divyāvadāna.
(A-av 126) In the *Aśokāvadāna*, when King Aśoka had gained faith in the teaching of the Blessed One, he spoke to the monks:
"By whom has much been given as a gift in the teaching of the Blessed One?
The monks replied,
"By the householder Anāthapiṇḍada."
The king asked,
"How much alms was given by him in the teaching of the Blessed One?
The monks replied:
He gave a hundred koṭis as an offering to the teaching of the Blessed One.
Upon hearing this, King Aśoka reflected:
"Having been that householder, he gave a hundred koṭis as an offering to the teaching of the Blessed One."
He said,
"I too shall give a hundred koṭis as an offering in the teaching of the Blessed One.
By him, as many as eighty-four thousand *dharmarājikā* stūpas were established.
And everywhere hundreds of thousands were given;
at his birth, at the awakening, at the turning of the wheel of Dharma, and at the final nirvana—everywhere a hundred thousand was given.
A quinquennial festival was held.
And there, four hundred thousand [pieces of gold] were given;
three hundred thousand monks were fed,
among whom were one part consisting of Arhats, two parts of those in training (śaikṣas), and [the remainder for] virtuous ordinary persons (pṛthagjana-kalyāṇaka).

Having deposited the treasury, he entrusted the great earth, the harem, the assembly of ministers, himself, and Kunāla to the noble Saṅgha; then, having given four hundred thousand [pieces of gold], he redeemed them.
He gave ninety-six koṭis as an offering to the teaching of the Blessed One.
Eventually, he fell ill.
Then the king, thinking "I shall no longer exist," became overwhelmed with distress.
His minister named Rādhagupta, with whom he had once shared the gift of sand,
seeing King Aśoka thus distressed, prostrated at his feet and, with palms joined in reverence, said:

O Lord, why is your face bathed in tears, though it possesses the splendor of a hundred lotus-faces and shines like the fierce sun— a face that could not even be gazed upon when encountered by hosts of powerful enemies?
The king said: "Rādhagupta, I do not grieve for the loss of wealth, nor for the loss of my kingdom, nor for separation from my refuge;
rather, I grieve."
"O Noble Ones,
I shall separate myself from that Saṅgha which is endowed with all virtues, which is honored by both men and gods, and which stands before me."
"I shall honor him with excellent food and drink"—thinking this, these tears were released from me.
Moreover, Rādhagupta,
this was my heart’s desire:
"I shall give a gift of one hundred crores to the teaching of the Blessed One."
And that intention of mine was not yet fulfilled;
therefore, King Aśoka began to send gold and bullion to the Kukkuṭārāma, thinking, "I shall complete the four crores.
At that time, Kunāla’s son, named Saṃpati, was serving as the crown prince.
The ministers said to him,
"Prince, King Aśoka will remain for only a short time;
furthermore, this wealth is being sent to the Kukkuṭārāma."
Kings who possess the strength of a treasury must be restrained; thus,
the prince prohibited the treasurer.
When King Aśoka’s prosperity was unchecked, food was served to him in golden vessels;
having eaten, he would send those golden vessels to the Kukkuṭārāma.
Then, the use of golden vessels was prohibited for him.
Food was served in silver vessels;
he even sent those away to the Kukkuṭārāma. Thereupon, the silver vessel was also prohibited.
While food was being served to him from an earthen bowl,
at that moment, half of an *āmalaka* fruit came into King Aśoka’s hand.
Then King Aśoka, deeply moved, assembled his ministers and the citizens and said:
"Who now is the lord upon the earth?
Then the ministers rose from their seats, bowed with palms joined toward King Aśoka, and said:
"Your Majesty, [you] are the lord upon the earth."
Then King Aśoka, his face and eyes clouded with tears, said to his ministers:
"Why do you speak such a falsehood out of courtesy? We have fallen from our sovereign power; all that remains of my lordship is this single *āmala* fruit."
Fie upon this ignoble sovereignty of mine, a lord of mortals, which is like entering the surging waters of a river; for even for me, poverty has arrived, bringing with it terror.

Alternatively, who could possibly act contrary to the word of the Blessed One? For it was asserted by Gautama, the speaker of truth, that all prosperities are the cause of misfortunes; and this has not proven false.

My command shall be carried out by you before long; for today, as soon as I have mentally resolved it upon the surface of this great mountain rock, the river that was obstructed by you will flow back again.

Having commanded that the earth be made one under a single umbrella, with its riots and tumults dispelled, having uprooted the hosts of arrogant enemies and comforted the wretched and the afflicted—[this shall be done].
Now that his foundation has crumbled, the wretched King Aśoka no longer shines; like a withered aśoka tree whose leaves and flowers have fallen, faded, and shattered, he now withers away.
Then King Aśoka, having summoned a man who was standing nearby, said:
"Good sir, out of affection for my former virtues, perform this final service for me even though I have fallen from my sovereignty.
Take this half-amalaka fruit of mine, go to the Kukkuṭārāma, and offer it to the Saṅgha."
And by my word, having performed prostrations at the feet of the Saṅgha, you should say:
"This is now the sovereign wealth of the King of Jambudvīpa.
Furthermore, this final gift should be enjoyed in such a way that my offering to the Saṅgha may become extensive. And he said:
This is my final gift today; both my kingdom and that [body] have returned to their own nature.
For one deprived of health, physicians, and medicine, there is no protector for me outside of the Noble Assembly.
Let it be eaten in such a way that this may be my final act of giving,
so that today my extensive offering to the Saṅgha may be fulfilled.

"So be it, Your Majesty," that man replied to King Aśoka. Taking half of the *āmalaka* fruit, he went to the Kukkutārāma monastery and, standing before the elders with palms joined in reverence, offered the half-*āmalaka* to the Saṅgha, saying:
"He who formerly commanded the earth under a single raised umbrella—"
Just as the sun at midday scorches the world by day, so did he [formerly] scorch it;
but today, having observed a breach in his fortune and being deprived of his own merits, that king stands at the close of day like the sun, its radiance fallen away.
Having prostrated with his head bowed in devotion before the Saṅgha, he indeed gave this half of an āmalaka fruit, marked by the fickleness of fortune.
Thereupon, the Elder of the Saṅgha said to the monks:
"Venerable sirs, it is now possible for you to give rise to a sense of spiritual urgency."
For thus it was said by the Blessed One: "The misfortune of others is a ground for spiritual urgency. Now, what person of sensitive heart would not experience such urgency? Why? Why? (A-av 131)
This king Aśoka, a hero in renunciation and an elephant among the Moryas,
having been the sovereign of Jambudvīpa, was born as the lord of Ardhamalaka.
Today that lord of the earth, his authority having been seized by his servants,
gives away only this half of an *āmalaka* fruit as a gift—
alas, for those who were exceedingly arrogant with the pride of the expansion of wealth and enjoyments!
As if repudiating the minds of ordinary people.
When half of that *āmalaka* fruit had been ground into powder and added to the soup, which was then distributed among the Saṅgha,
King Aśoka said to Rādhagupta:
"Tell me, Rādhagupta, who is now the lord of the earth?"
Then Rādhagupta, prostrating at the feet of Aśoka with palms joined in reverence, said:
"The Lord is the sovereign upon the earth.
Then King Aśoka, having somehow risen and looked toward the four quarters, joined his palms toward the Saṅgha and said:
Having now established this great treasury, I offer this entire great earth, bounded by the oceans, to the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples. And he said:
"This earth, clad in the dark-blue mantle of the supreme ocean, its face adorned with many mines of jewels..."
I give this earth, together with the oceans, to that Saṅgha; let its fruit be enjoyed.
Moreover:
"By this gift, I do not seek the abode of Indra, nor the fruit in the world of Brahmā."
I long for royal splendor, which is as fickle as the rush of swift water,
only because of this fruit of my giving honored by devotion; may I thereby attain the sovereignty of mind, revered by the noble, which never undergoes transformation.
After the document had been written out and sealed with a tooth-seal,
the king passed away after having bestowed the great earth upon the Saṅgha.
Then the ministers, having carried him out on blue and yellow litters, performed the funeral rites for his body, cremated him, and said, "We shall install [another] king."
When Rādhagupta announced,
"King Aśoka has bestowed the great earth upon the Saṅgha," the ministers then asked, "For what purpose?"
Rādhagupta said:
"This was King Aśoka’s aspiration: 'I shall give a gift of one hundred koṭis to the teaching of the Blessed One.
By him, ninety-six koṭis have been given."
When the command was thus forbidden,
the king, with that intention, gave the great earth to the Saṅgha.
Subsequently, the ministers, having given four koṭis to the teaching of the Blessed One, redeemed the earth and reinstated Saṃpati in the kingdom.
Saṃpadin had a son, Bṛhaspati; Bṛhaspati’s was Vṛṣasena; Vṛṣasena’s was Puṣyadharman; and Puṣyadharman’s was Puṣyamitra.
He addressed his ministers:
"What means might there be so that our name may endure for a long time?
They replied,
"In the lineage of Your Majesty, there was a king named Aśoka."
By him, eighty-four thousand *dharmarājikā* stupas were established; his fame shall endure for as long as the teaching of the Blessed One remains.
"May Your Majesty also establish eighty-four thousand *dharmarājikā* stupas.
The king said, "King Aśoka was one of great majesty."
"There must be some other means.
His brahmin domestic chaplain was an ordinary person who lacked faith;
he said:
"Your Majesty, for two reasons its name will endure for a long time:
because King Aśoka has established eighty-four thousand *dharmarājikā* stupas, its name will remain for a long time;
and if you were to destroy them, your own name would endure even longer."
When King Puṣyamitra, having mobilized his fourfold army, set out for the Kukkuṭārāma with the intention of destroying the teaching of the Blessed One,
a lion’s roar was let loose at the gate;
thereupon, the king, terrified, entered Pāṭaliputra.
Thus he spoke a second and a third time;
finally, having summoned the monks and the Saṅgha, he said,
"I shall destroy the teaching of the Blessed One."
"Do you wish for a stūpa or monasteries?
Stūpas have already been accepted by the monks."
When Puṣyamitra had set out, destroying the monasteries and slaughtering the monks,
he eventually reached Śākala. Thereupon, he spoke:

"Whoever shall give me the head of a śramaṇa, to him I will give a hundred dīnāras. Thereupon, a certain arhat residing at a Dharmarājikā monastery began to offer his head through supernatural power (ṛddhi). Upon hearing this, the king began to have the arhat executed.
And he had entered into the attainment of cessation;
no assault from another could affect him. Having abandoned that state, he went as far as the storehouse.
The yakṣa Daṃṣṭrānivāsin thought:
"This teaching of the Blessed One is perishing,
yet I uphold the training."
"I am unable to do anything displeasing to anyone.
His daughter has been requested by the yakṣa Kṛmiśa,
yet he does not grant her, saying, 'You are a doer of evil deeds.'"
Eventually, that daughter was given by him to Kṛmiśa for the sake of protecting the teaching of the Blessed One and for the sake of upholding and guarding [the community].
A yakṣa of immense size followed behind King Puṣyamitra.
By the power of that [yakṣa], the king was not obstructed;
meanwhile, the yakṣa Daṃṣṭrānivāsin seized the yakṣa who had followed Puṣyamitra and wandered about on the mountain.
He proceeded as far as the great southern ocean.
Then the yakṣa Kṛmiśa brought a massive mountain and hemmed in King Puṣyamitra along with his army and vehicles;
he was given the name Sunihita.
When King Puṣyamitra was put to death, the Maurya dynasty was completely extinguished.
Thus ends the "Aśoka-avadāna" in the glorious Divyāvadāna.
